projects.title: Accuracy vs. Interpretability in Designer-Level Fashion Classification
projects.subtitle: Image classification for apparel categories
projects.summary: Built a classifier that tags clothing items from images for rapid cataloging.

glance.oneLiner: Designer-level fashion classification that probes the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability.
glance.problem: Models can achieve high accuracy on runway images but often rely on background shortcuts instead of garment cues.
glance.approach: Compare ResNet baselines with custom FashionNet-Small/Medium across three regimes: unmasked images, segmentation-based background removal, and heavy augmentation. Use Grad-CAM and nearest-neighbor retrieval to evaluate what the models attend to.
glance.results: Unmasked training yields the best accuracy (pretrained ResNet-50 ~94%) but relies on background. Masking shifts attention to garments yet drops accuracy (pretrained ResNet-50 ~84%, FashionNet-Small near chance). Heavy augmentation reduces shortcut learning while recovering performance.
takeaways: Background removal improves interpretability but hurts low-capacity models
Model capacity matters when contextual cues are stripped away
Augmentation helps but does not fully eliminate background reliance

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Designer-level fashion classification is a fine-grained recognition problem with a twist: the garment is the label, but the runway often becomes the cue. Strong accuracy can hide shortcut learning when models rely on lighting, venue layout, and floor textures instead of clothing.

This project evaluates how model capacity and training strategy affect both performance and interpretability on the iDesigner FGVC dataset, using Grad-CAM and feature-space retrieval to see what the models actually learn.

callout.label: Key finding
callout.text: Unmasked training yields high accuracy but heavy background reliance. Masking improves garment-centric attention but causes large drops for low-capacity models. Aggressive augmentation helps but does not fully remove shortcuts.

sections.title: Dataset
paragraphs: We use the iDesigner FGVC dataset (CVPR 2019), containing 50,000 high-resolution runway images labeled by designer across major fashion houses. Images are cropped around the model but preserve runway context, which introduces strong background correlations.

To isolate garment-level signals, we build a background-subtracted dataset using DeepLab person segmentation. This preprocessing removes runway pixels and preserves the model and garments to better evaluate garment-centric learning.

sections.title: Model Architectures
paragraphs: We evaluate three families of CNNs: ResNet-18/34/50 baselines and two lightweight custom models, FashionNet-Small and FashionNet-Medium. The custom models are designed to emphasize local textures and silhouettes while remaining more interpretable than large residual networks.

tables.title: Table I: Number of learnable parameters per architecture

sections.title: Methods
paragraphs: We compare ResNet baselines against FashionNet-Small and FashionNet-Medium across three training regimes: unmasked images, masked images, and heavy augmentation on unmasked data.
Interpretability is assessed with Grad-CAM and nearest-neighbor retrieval in feature space to verify whether embeddings cluster by garment attributes rather than background cues.
bullets: Phase I: Baseline training on unmasked images (high accuracy, shortcut risk).
Phase II: Masked training with background removed (garment-centric attention, accuracy drop).
Phase III: Heavy augmentation on unmasked data (partial mitigation without explicit masking).

sections.title: Results: Phase I (Unmasked)
paragraphs: Training on the original runway images yields strong accuracy, especially for pretrained ResNet-50. Qualitative Grad-CAM inspection shows that many models attend to runway and lighting rather than the garment itself.

tables.title: Table II: Validation accuracy (%) on the unmasked dataset

sections.title: Results: Phase II (Masked)
paragraphs: Background removal via segmentation forces networks to rely on garment shape and texture. Accuracy drops substantially across all architectures, especially for the lightweight FashionNet variants.
Grad-CAM becomes more garment-centered for masked training, indicating reduced reliance on contextual cues.

tables.title: Table III: Validation accuracy (%) on the masked dataset

sections.title: Results: Phase III (Heavy Augmentation)
paragraphs: Strong augmentation (crop/resize, color jitter, flips, perspective transforms, random erasing, and noise masks) weakens background correlations without masking. Performance recovers relative to the masked setting, but shortcut cues remain visible in Grad-CAM.

tables.title: Table IV: Validation accuracy (%) with strong augmentation on unmasked data

sections.title: Feature-Space Interpretability
paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor retrieval using FashionNet-Medium trained on masked images suggests embeddings organize by meaningful garment attributes such as color, texture, and silhouette even when background returns at test time.
This supports the interpretability claim: masking promotes garment-centric representations, even if it comes at an accuracy cost.

sections.title: Takeaways
bullets: Accuracy can be misleading: on unmasked runway images, models often win by learning the venue.
Masking improves interpretability but harms low-capacity models most.
Augmentation helps reduce shortcuts, but does not fully eliminate background reliance.
Capacity and pretraining matter when contextual cues are removed.
